n: Mormon jumps forward: while traveling south toward Manti, Alma unexpectedly meets the sons of Mosiah returning home after fourteen years. Chapters 17–26 then flash back to tell their story.

f.g: This reunion took place about 77 BC; the story that follows starts about 91 BC.

n: Alma rejoices: these old companions from the angel’s visit are still faithful, strong in the truth, and diligent students of the scriptures.
They also gave themselves to much prayer and fasting, so they had the spirit of prophecy and revelation and taught with God’s power and authority — a model for every missionary.
For fourteen years they taught the Lamanites and brought many to God’s altar to confess their sins.

f.g: About 91–77 BC.

n: Their mission was hard: hunger, thirst, fatigue, and much spiritual labor.
They had left in the first year of the judges, having refused the throne their father and the people wanted them to take.
They took weapons for hunting food in the wilderness, not for war.
With their chosen companions they headed into the wilderness toward the land of Nephi.

f.w: their numbers which they had selected

n: Along the way they fasted and prayed for the Spirit to go with them, hoping to help the Lamanites see their fathers’ incorrect traditions.

f.w: an instrument in the hands of God

f.g: Lowness; lack of worth.

n: The Lord comforted them by his Spirit: “Be comforted.” And they were.

f.g: A short, tender message — sometimes all that is needed.

n: The Lord sends them out with a charge: be patient in suffering, set a good example, and he will make them instruments in saving many.

f.w: show forth good examples unto them in me

n: Encouraged, they set out with courage to preach.
At the Lamanite border they split up, trusting they would reunite at the end of their “harvest.”

f.g: A farming metaphor for missionary work.

n: Mormon describes how daunting their task was: the Lamanites of that time were fierce, delighted in killing Nephites, and sought wealth by plunder rather than work.

f.w: a wild and a hardened and a ferocious people

n: Many were idle and worshiped idols, under a curse because of their fathers’ traditions — yet the Lord’s promises remained open to them if they repented.

f.g: Lazy, idle.

f.w: the promises of the Lord were extended unto them

n: That is precisely why the sons of Mosiah went: to bring them to repentance and teach them the plan of redemption.
Each went alone, relying on God’s word and power.

f.g: Unlike modern missionaries who usually serve in pairs, they separated to cover more ground.

n: Ammon, their leader, blessed and instructed each of them before they parted.

f.g: According to each one’s assignment.

n: Ammon goes to the land of Ishmael, named for Ishmael’s descendants who had joined the Lamanites.
Lamanites seize and bind Ammon, as was their custom with Nephites, and bring him before the king, who could kill, imprison, enslave, or expel him.
The king of the land is Lamoni, a descendant of Ishmael.
Lamoni asks whether Ammon wants to live among his people.

f.g: A surprisingly mild question to a captured Nephite.

n: Ammon says yes — perhaps for the rest of his life. He has come to stay.

f.w: perhaps until the day I die
f.g: A sign of complete commitment.

n: Lamoni is so pleased that he frees Ammon and offers him one of his daughters in marriage.

f.w: take one of his daughters to wife
f.g: A sign of great favor that would have made Ammon royal family.

n: Ammon declines and instead offers to be Lamoni’s servant. He is set to tend the king’s flocks. Service, not status, opens hearts.
Three days later, Ammon and other servants drive the flocks to the water of Sebus, the common watering place.

f.g: A shared watering place for Lamanite flocks.

n: A gang of Lamanites scatters the king’s flocks in every direction — apparently a common form of theft.
The servants panic and weep: the king has executed earlier servants whose flocks were scattered.
Ammon’s heart swells with joy — he sees a chance to show God’s power, win his fellow servants’ hearts, and lead them to believe.

f.w: that I may win the hearts
f.g: Ammon sees the crisis as a door to teach, not only a problem to solve.

n: These were Ammon’s thoughts as he saw the suffering of those he called his brothers.

f.g: Ammon thinks of the Lamanite servants as family.

n: He reassures them: be of good cheer; let’s round up the flocks so the king won’t kill us.

f.g: Here, encouraged or spoke kindly — not deceitfully.

n: They follow Ammon, race ahead of the flocks, and gather them back to the water.

f.g: Got ahead of them to turn them back.

n: The thieves return. Ammon tells the servants to circle the flocks while he confronts the men alone.

f.g: Ammon organizes and leads.

n: The servants obey, and Ammon faces a large group.

f.g: A sizable number.

n: The men don’t fear one Nephite. They don’t know the Lord had promised Mosiah to protect his sons.
Ammon slings stones with great power, killing some. Unable to hit him with their stones, the rest charge with clubs.
Ammon uses his sword to strike off the arms of each attacker who raised a club. Astonished, they flee.

f.g: A defensive strike aimed at the raised weapon arms.

n: Six fell by the sling; only their leader was killed by the sword. Many arms were cut off.

f.w: he slew none save it were their leader
f.g: Ammon used restraint even in combat.

n: The flocks are watered and returned. The servants bring the severed arms to the king as evidence of what happened.

f.g: Evidence to prove their remarkable story.
